Recommended checks: Compare vibration (mm/s), machine temperature (\u00b0F), motor load (%), and factory air temperature (\u00b0F) over the same relevant time window. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (\u00a72.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (\u00a72.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. decisions.information_needed: what to find out first
Per-tick CNC-02 vibration from just before the alarm to now, to confirm persistence vs isolated spike (Q1).
Line-wide events around the alarm time: CNC-02 running/idle state, job changes, setting changes, maintenance, stops (Q3, Q5).
CNC-02 temperature trend across the same window as the vibration spikes (900-920), to test bearing-deterioration vs sensor-disturbance
CNC-07 vibration trend from 900 to 920 to check for a rising trend.
CNC-07 load trend from 900 to 920 to check for a rising trend.
CNC-08 vibration trend from 900 to 920 to check for a rising trend.

What the evidence settled: Q4-recheck — CNC-02 temperature stays essentially flat across 900-920 (E6: delta +0.70°F over the window; max 147.95°F occurred at tick 906, not at the 914/919 vibration spikes; value at 914 is 146.66°F, mid-range), so there is no temperature rise correlated with the vibration alarms → supports H2 over H1. Q5 — event log 880-914 (E5) shows no CNC-02 setting change, speed change, job/workpiece change, or maintenance before the alarm → none found. Other machines checked: CNC-07 and CNC-08 show only mild, stable elevations (E7-E9: vibration means 2.428/2.413, load mean 75.824; no rising trend), far below CNC-02's screening scores, so no shared rising line effect → H3 not supported. Leading explanation: H2 — CNC-02's alarms are isolated/recurring vibration transients without a corroborating rising temperature trend and with no preceding setting/maintenance change. Caveat: E2 screening shows CNC-02 persistently above baseline in vibration ([7.87, 8.32]) and steady-hot temperature ([6.58, 6.25, steady]); per manual §2.1 a persistent change across independent signals merits deeper monitoring or a physical inspection rather than an immediate bearing repair, and vibration alone does not diagnose a bearing. No open questions remain; further calls would be redundant (Q4 already answered by E6, Q5 by E5, other machines already checked).
what could explain the evidence
Status of every machine and CNC-02's state during the vibration window; nearby-machine anomalies for Q7
Any maintenance visit on CNC-02 before tick 914 (during the run or in the months prior), which would support H3 as an operational/maintenance-related cause.
When job 12 started, on which machines it ran, and whether it represents a recent job/workpiece change on CNC-02 before tick 914, which would support H3.

Q4-recheck is settled by existing evidence: CNC-02 temperature stays flat across 900-920 (delta +0.7 °F over the window, min 144.4 °F, max 147.9 °F, no rise at the 914/919 vibration spikes; E2 also reports temperature 'steady'). This separates H1 (mechanical fault: vibration + rising temperature) from H2 (isolated transients, flat temperature) in favor of H2. A complete line scan via E2 shows CNC-02 is the only machine with alarm-level vibration (screening scores 7.87/8.32); CNC-07 and CNC-08 show modestly elevated scores but raw vibration ~2.4 mm/s (below the 4.5 mm/s alarm) with steady temperatures, so no second fault is indicated. Per the manual (§2.1), a single spike without corroboration does not justify a repair.

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.13", "text": "When to consult: Pass/fail outcomes worsen; alarms persist; a proposed fix is uncertain; a recent maintenance action appears not to help. Possible causes: Material or process changes, equipment wear, speed error, tool or fixture faults, inspection variation, or coincidental multiple causes. Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (\u00a72.2), a speed-setting reset (\u00a72.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (\u00a72.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (\u00a72.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. \"Insufficient evidence\" or \"continue observing\" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Completion of work is not proof the root cause was correct.", "title": "Inspection Rejects, Maintenance Decisions and Verification"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.7", "text": "When to consult: Cycle times or quality change on one station; more or less vibration or heat after a setup; unexpectedly fast or slow work at one station. Possible causes: Incorrect program or setup speed, operator setting mistake, incorrect tooling recommendation, speed variation under load or mechanical drag. Recommended checks: The settings record shows a station's current speed only; its nominal speed is on the station's setup sheet, not in the shared records. So find a wrong setting from its effects. First, look for a change point: on one station, job times, temperature and inspection rejects shift at about the same moment and then stay at their new level, unlike wear, which keeps getting worse. Second, read the direction: a speed set too high shortens jobs and adds a little vibration and heat; a speed set too low lengthens jobs and takes a little vibration and heat away; either way, more jobs fail inspection. A worn bearing, by contrast, lengthens jobs while vibration rises. Third, compare with the other stations: a material problem spreads across stations that handle the same batch, a setting stays on one station. Verify that a slow cycle is not simply a downstream blockage (\u00a72.8). How to interpret: A change point with these effects on one station is a configuration clue, not proof that it caused every anomaly. The corrective action is an approved setting reset, which stops the station for about 10 ticks and returns it to its nominal speed. Because it is short and reversible, it is also a test: if job times, temperature and rejects return to their earlier levels afterwards, the setting was the cause; if not, look again.", "title": "Spindle Speed Configuration and Machining Effects"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.9", "text": "When to consult: Inspection rejects cluster by batch or appear on jobs processed across several otherwise stable machines. Possible causes: Incoming stock variation, material hardness or contamination, a supplier or heat-treatment issue, cutting conditions, tooling, machine settings, or inspection randomness. Recommended checks: Group pass/fail results by batch ID; compare multiple jobs and adjacent batches. Trace representative rejected jobs through the line and check whether the same station or setting coincides with rejects. When possible, request material certificates, dimensional checks and receiving inspection rather than treating the lot number as an answer. How to interpret: Batch IDs connect material and finished jobs; a defect rate is statistical, so one failed inspection is weak evidence. A bad lot raises the share of rejects; it does not make every part fail, so jobs from that lot that pass inspection do not clear it, and an alternating or other pattern among a few jobs is usually chance. Judge a batch by its reject rate against other batches run through the same stations: a clearly higher rate in one batch points at the material even when some of its jobs pass. Material can be suspect even if equipment sensor trends remain normal, but also consider machine or inspection causes.", "title": "Material Batch Quality and Lot Traceability"}]

conclusion.diagnosis: Intermittent inspection rejections on alternating batch-2 jobs (jobs 11, 13, 15 failed; jobs 12, 14 passed; batch-1 job 10 passed). A real recurring defect is indicated, but it is not localized to CNC-06: each failed job was last machined on CNC-06 immediately before its failed inspection, yet CNC-06 following_error and vibration are normal while jobs 11/13/15 are being cut (means ≈3.4–3.9) and actually rise during passed job 12 (means ≈5.0–5.1), so CNC-06 axis behavior does not track the failures (E7, E8, E11, E12). CNC-05 blocking damage is inconsistent — job 12 was blocked at CNC-05 yet passed (E9, E10). CNC-01–CNC-04 were never compared in their failed-job versus passed-job processing windows (E13–E16 retrieved but not examined in detail), and an inspection-station or material-lot alternation cannot be excluded. Root cause: unresolved.

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.7", "text": "When to consult: Cycle times or quality change on one station; more or less vibration or heat after a setup; unexpectedly fast or slow work at one station. Possible causes: Incorrect program or setup speed, operator setting mistake, incorrect tooling recommendation, speed variation under load or mechanical drag. Recommended checks: The settings record shows a station's current speed only; its nominal speed is on the station's setup sheet, not in the shared records. So find a wrong setting from its effects. First, look for a change point: on one station, job times, temperature and inspection rejects shift at about the same moment and then stay at their new level, unlike wear, which keeps getting worse. Second, read the direction: a speed set too high shortens jobs and adds a little vibration and heat; a speed set too low lengthens jobs and takes a little vibration and heat away; either way, more jobs fail inspection. A worn bearing, by contrast, lengthens jobs while vibration rises. Third, compare with the other stations: a material problem spreads across stations that handle the same batch, a setting stays on one station. Verify that a slow cycle is not simply a downstream blockage (\u00a72.8). How to interpret: A change point with these effects on one station is a configuration clue, not proof that it caused every anomaly. The corrective action is an approved setting reset, which stops the station for about 10 ticks and returns it to its nominal speed. Because it is short and reversible, it is also a test: if job times, temperature and rejects return to their earlier levels afterwards, the setting was the cause; if not, look again.", "title": "Spindle Speed Configuration and Machining Effects"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.9", "text": "When to consult: Inspection rejects cluster by batch or appear on jobs processed across several otherwise stable machines. Possible causes: Incoming stock variation, material hardness or contamination, a supplier or heat-treatment issue, cutting conditions, tooling, machine settings, or inspection randomness. Recommended checks: Group pass/fail results by batch ID; compare multiple jobs and adjacent batches. Trace representative rejected jobs through the line and check whether the same station or setting coincides with rejects. When possible, request material certificates, dimensional checks and receiving inspection rather than treating the lot number as an answer. How to interpret: Batch IDs connect material and finished jobs; a defect rate is statistical, so one failed inspection is weak evidence. A bad lot raises the share of rejects; it does not make every part fail, so jobs from that lot that pass inspection do not clear it, and an alternating or other pattern among a few jobs is usually chance. Judge a batch by its reject rate against other batches run through the same stations: a clearly higher rate in one batch points at the material even when some of its jobs pass. Material can be suspect even if equipment sensor trends remain normal, but also consider machine or inspection causes.", "title": "Material Batch Quality and Lot Traceability"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.13", "text": "When to consult: Pass/fail outcomes worsen; alarms persist; a proposed fix is uncertain; a recent maintenance action appears not to help. Possible causes: Material or process changes, equipment wear, speed error, tool or fixture faults, inspection variation, or coincidental multiple causes. Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (\u00a72.2), a speed-setting reset (\u00a72.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (\u00a72.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (\u00a72.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. \"Insufficient evidence\" or \"continue observing\" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Completion of work is not proof the root cause was correct.", "title": "Inspection Rejects, Maintenance Decisions and Verification"}]

hypotheses.claim: Single-station configuration fault (e.g., wrong spindle-speed setting) with a step change around job 11 in cycle time/temperature/rejects, confined to one station.
expected_observations: Failed jobs share one station showing a step shift around job 11 while other stations do not.
assumptions: All failed jobs passed through CNC-01..CNC-06; manual's setting-vs-wear distinction applies.
hypotheses.discriminating_check: Compare per-job cycle times and sensor readings at each station before vs after job 11; check get_settings speeds; rule out blockage.

hypotheses.claim: Material/batch problem spreading across stations handling the same batch; failures cluster by batch, not machine.
expected_observations: Jobs 11-13 share a material batch that earlier passed jobs did not; failures track batch_id across stations.
assumptions: Inspection results carry material-batch identifiers; batch 2 jobs all failed.
hypotheses.discriminating_check: Confirm batch_ids of jobs 1-13 and whether any batch-1 job failed; check if failures track batch rather than a single station.

hypotheses.claim: Downstream blockage coinciding with slow cycle/rejects: CNC-02 blocks CNC-01 (CNC-01 starved/blocked), new or worsened at job 11, not a station setting.
expected_observations: Block/stop/starve events around jobs 11-13; CNC-02 blocked while CNC-01 starves; pattern new at job 11 rather than chronic.
assumptions: Manual §2.7 blockage check applies; CNC-02 is the downstream station blocking CNC-01.
hypotheses.discriminating_check: Compare block/starve events around jobs 11-13 vs earlier jobs; compare CNC-02 cycle times before/after job 11.

conclusion.diagnosis: Pending evidence: jobs 11–13 (batch 2) all fail inspection while jobs 1–10 (batch 1) all pass; every job routes through CNC-01→CNC-02→CNC-03→CNC-04→CNC-05→CNC-06 before inspection, so any station or the batch itself is a candidate. Rival hypotheses: H1 single-station setting fault with step change at job 11, H2 batch-2 material problem affecting all stations, H3 downstream blockage at CNC-02 worsening at job 11. Cycle times observed so far (job 1 vs job 11) look similar, but I need a direct job-10 vs job-11 comparison to detect a step change at any station, plus whether CNC-02 blocking is new at job 11.

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.13", "text": "When to consult: Pass/fail outcomes worsen; alarms persist; a proposed fix is uncertain; a recent maintenance action appears not to help. Possible causes: Material or process changes, equipment wear, speed error, tool or fixture faults, inspection variation, or coincidental multiple causes. Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (\u00a72.2), a speed-setting reset (\u00a72.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (\u00a72.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (\u00a72.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. \"Insufficient evidence\" or \"continue observing\" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Completion of work is not proof the root cause was correct.", "title": "Inspection Rejects, Maintenance Decisions and Verification"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.14", "text": "When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (\u00a72.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (\u00a72.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. The corrective action is an approved servo drive replacement, which takes the station out of service for about an hour; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the drive removed, which is direct evidence of whether it was worn. Afterwards, following error during running work should return to a few micrometres and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again (an instrument, a binding axis or a second fault).", "title": "Feed-Axis Servo Drive: Following Error, Wear and Replacement"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a71.2", "text": "When to consult: A sensor exceeds an alarm value; averages disagree across windows; a trend looks erratic or has gaps. Possible causes: Operating changes, transient disturbances, instrument issues or developing equipment problems. Recommended checks: Compare vibration (mm/s), machine temperature (\u00b0F), motor load (%), and factory air temperature (\u00b0F) over the same relevant time window. Record ticks, sample counts, minimum and maximum, and a trend, not only the last reading. Separate running from idle periods. Link alarms to the underlying sensor readings and independent evidence. How to interpret: The default line vibration alarm is triggered by a reading above 4.5 mm/s. It is a monitoring setpoint, not a confirmed failure threshold. Missing samples are unknown, never zero. A sensor reading and a maintenance note are evidence; neither is a diagnosis. Observable channels and records: vibration (mm/s per station; speed, load and instruments affect readings); temperature (\u00b0F per station; thermal lag, compare factory air); load (% per station; active machining against idle matters); air temperature (\u00b0F, factory-wide; door and daily variation); power (kW per station; cutting load and speed, plus friction or a straining drive); following error (\u00b5m per station, the feed axis's lag behind its commanded path; \u00a72.14); hydraulic pressure (bar, only on stations fitted with hydraulics; \u00a72.15); events and job history (alarms, job movement, stops; events record observations, not causes); inspections (job, batch, pass or fail; outcomes are statistical); settings and maintenance (the current speed only, and service notes; service history is not present health).", "title": "Measurements, Trends, Alarms and Evidence Quality"}]

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.13", "text": "When to consult: Pass/fail outcomes worsen; alarms persist; a proposed fix is uncertain; a recent maintenance action appears not to help. Possible causes: Material or process changes, equipment wear, speed error, tool or fixture faults, inspection variation, or coincidental multiple causes. Recommended checks: Build a time-aligned record: affected machine and job IDs, batches, speeds, sensor trends, alarms, prior service and inspection results. State competing explanations and what evidence would separate them. Select an available action only when the expected improvement and potential downtime are justified; obtain human approval before execution. After maintenance, compare the same operating signals and inspection outcomes over a meaningful subsequent window. How to interpret: On this line, the only state-changing interventions are four approved repairs: a spindle-bearing replacement (\u00a72.2), a speed-setting reset (\u00a72.7), a feed-axis servo drive replacement (\u00a72.14) and a hydraulic seal repair on a station fitted with hydraulics (\u00a72.15). Each fixes one mechanism only; none repairs material, tooling or an instrument. Other physical checks may require a technician and are not available as actions. \"Insufficient evidence\" or \"continue observing\" are legitimate conclusions when the evidence does not separate the causes, but a fault that keeps worsening does not clear by being watched: wear and leaks progress until repaired. Completion of work is not proof the root cause was correct.", "title": "Inspection Rejects, Maintenance Decisions and Verification"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.14", "text": "When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (\u00a72.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (\u00a72.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. The corrective action is an approved servo drive replacement, which takes the station out of service for about an hour; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the drive removed, which is direct evidence of whether it was worn. Afterwards, following error during running work should return to a few micrometres and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again (an instrument, a binding axis or a second fault).", "title": "Feed-Axis Servo Drive: Following Error, Wear and Replacement"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.7", "text": "When to consult: Cycle times or quality change on one station; more or less vibration or heat after a setup; unexpectedly fast or slow work at one station. Possible causes: Incorrect program or setup speed, operator setting mistake, incorrect tooling recommendation, speed variation under load or mechanical drag. Recommended checks: The settings record shows a station's current speed only; its nominal speed is on the station's setup sheet, not in the shared records. So find a wrong setting from its effects. First, look for a change point: on one station, job times, temperature and inspection rejects shift at about the same moment and then stay at their new level, unlike wear, which keeps getting worse. Second, read the direction: a speed set too high shortens jobs and adds a little vibration and heat; a speed set too low lengthens jobs and takes a little vibration and heat away; either way, more jobs fail inspection. A worn bearing, by contrast, lengthens jobs while vibration rises. Third, compare with the other stations: a material problem spreads across stations that handle the same batch, a setting stays on one station. Verify that a slow cycle is not simply a downstream blockage (\u00a72.8). How to interpret: A change point with these effects on one station is a configuration clue, not proof that it caused every anomaly. The corrective action is an approved setting reset, which stops the station for about 10 ticks and returns it to its nominal speed. Because it is short and reversible, it is also a test: if job times, temperature and rejects return to their earlier levels afterwards, the setting was the cause; if not, look again.", "title": "Spindle Speed Configuration and Machining Effects"}]

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.1", "text": "When to consult: One high vibration alarm; recurring peaks; a sustained increase in mm/s during production. Possible causes: Heavier workpiece load, speed change, spindle-bearing deterioration, imbalance, loose mounting, alignment, cutting chatter, or sensor disturbance. Recommended checks: Check whether the machine was running. Compare several consecutive readings and trend windows at similar loads and spindle speeds; look for changes in temperature or load. Check nearby stations for shared effects. Review operating events, setting changes, and prior maintenance. Request a physical inspection when telemetry does not separate mechanical vibration from sensor movement. How to interpret: A single spike without corroboration does not justify a repair. A persistent change across independent signals merits deeper investigation. Do not diagnose a bearing by vibration alone. See \u00a72.2, \u00a72.4 and \u00a72.11.", "title": "Abnormal Vibration: Spike, Step Change or Gradual Rise"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a71.2", "text": "When to consult: A sensor exceeds an alarm value; averages disagree across windows; a trend looks erratic or has gaps. Possible causes: Operating changes, transient disturbances, instrument issues or developing equipment problems. Recommended checks: Compare vibration (mm/s), machine temperature (\u00b0F), motor load (%), and factory air temperature (\u00b0F) over the same relevant time window. Record ticks, sample counts, minimum and maximum, and a trend, not only the last reading. Separate running from idle periods. Link alarms to the underlying sensor readings and independent evidence. How to interpret: The default line vibration alarm is triggered by a reading above 4.5 mm/s. It is a monitoring setpoint, not a confirmed failure threshold. Missing samples are unknown, never zero. A sensor reading and a maintenance note are evidence; neither is a diagnosis. Observable channels and records: vibration (mm/s per station; speed, load and instruments affect readings); temperature (\u00b0F per station; thermal lag, compare factory air); load (% per station; active machining against idle matters); air temperature (\u00b0F, factory-wide; door and daily variation); power (kW per station; cutting load and speed, plus friction or a straining drive); following error (\u00b5m per station, the feed axis's lag behind its commanded path; \u00a72.14); hydraulic pressure (bar, only on stations fitted with hydraulics; \u00a72.15); events and job history (alarms, job movement, stops; events record observations, not causes); inspections (job, batch, pass or fail; outcomes are statistical); settings and maintenance (the current speed only, and service notes; service history is not present health).", "title": "Measurements, Trends, Alarms and Evidence Quality"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.14", "text": "When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Check vibration, temperature and job times: a worn drive leaves them unchanged, while a worn spindle bearing raises vibration and heat and lengthens jobs (\u00a72.2), and a wrong speed changes job times at one moment and then holds them steady (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by the station each failed job passed through: a drive fault follows the station across material batches, while a bad lot follows the batch across stations (\u00a72.9). How to interpret: A lagging axis cuts parts off size, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the drive wears; as with any defect rate, some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A following error that keeps rising during production does not recover by itself and is not a transient: it keeps worsening until the drive is replaced, and an alarm that briefly clears is not evidence the drive is sound. The corrective action is an approved servo drive replacement, which takes the station out of service for about an hour; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the drive removed, which is direct evidence of whether it was worn. Afterwards, following error during running work should return to a few micrometres and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again (an instrument, a binding axis or a second fault).", "title": "Feed-Axis Servo Drive: Following Error, Wear and Replacement"}]

A sensor reading and a maintenance note are evidence; neither is a diagnosis. Observable channels and records: vibration (mm/s per station; speed, load and instruments affect readings); temperature (\u00b0F per station; thermal lag, compare factory air); load (% per station; active machining against idle matters); air temperature (\u00b0F, factory-wide; door and daily variation); power (kW per station; cutting load and speed, plus friction or a straining drive); following error (\u00b5m per station, the feed axis's lag behind its commanded path; \u00a72.14); hydraulic pressure (bar, only on stations fitted with hydraulics; \u00a72.15); events and job history (alarms, job movement, stops; events record observations, not causes); inspections (job, batch, pass or fail; outcomes are statistical); settings and maintenance (the current speed only, and service notes; service history is not present health).", "title": "Measurements, Trends, Alarms and Evidence Quality"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.14", "text": "When to consult: A following-error alarm; following error rising over many readings on one station; parts from one station failing inspection for size while its vibration and temperature stay normal. Possible causes: A wearing feed-axis servo drive (amplifier, motor or its feedback), a heavy cut, a faster speed setting, a binding axis, or an instrument fault on the axis channel. Recommended checks: Following error is how far the feed axis lags behind the position the controller commands, measured by the servo controller itself on every move. A healthy drive keeps it small, a few micrometres at normal load; a heavier cut or a faster speed adds a little; while a station is idle or stopped the drive only holds the axis still and the lag falls to about one micrometre, so compare running periods only. The alarm fires above 20 \u00b5m. A wearing drive adds lag that grows slowly at first and then faster, and only while the station runs: a harder job wears it faster. Read the trend on the affected station over a long running window, and compare it with the same channel on other stations. Check power on the same station: a straining drive draws a little more. Full machine inventory: which machines have hydraulics, and each machine's current running/idle/down state and current job.

Give CNC-05 more blocked/idle time so its hydraulic pressure can be observed over a longer idle window; determines whether the pressure keeps drifting below 55 bar while the station is not cutting.
CNC-05 hydraulic_pressure values during the post-wait idle window: does the trend stay below 55 bar and keep falling, or flatten above it?

The discriminating check has been completed by E10: during CNC-05's idle window (ticks 1290-1302), hydraulic_pressure stayed between 55.96 and 58.25 bar (mean 57.29, delta -0.10 bar), always above the 55 bar setpoint and roughly flat. This contradicts H1's core prediction (continuing fall below 55 bar even while idle) and matches H3 (idle pressure recovers/stays above setpoint; low pressure shows mainly under cut load). E6 places the sub-55 alarm reading (54.29 at tick 1281, min of bucket 1270-1290 in E5) while CNC-05 was cutting job 15 (ran 1231-1288, then blocked/idle at 1289). E2 shows CNC-05 hydraulic_pressure far below baseline under cut (scores -13.38/-13.53) while CNC-02, the only other hydraulic machine, is normal (scores 0.21/0.20), so the fault is localized and real, not an erratic transducer fault (readings are consistent across E5/E7/E10) and not line-wide. The long-term idle baseline has degraded (~63.5 bar mean at ticks 1000-1029 to ~57.3 bar at 1290-1302), but it is not breaching 55 during idle. Conclusion: H3 is the leading explanation; H1 is contradicted by E10; H_instrument is unsupported. No further call would change this diagnosis.
what could explain the evidence

What the evidence settled: CNC-05's hydraulic system is genuinely degraded (H2). E5 shows idle steady-state pressure fell from ~63.5 bar (ticks 1000-1029) to ~57-58 bar (ticks 1270-1302), a real decline not a one-off fluctuation. The sub-55 bar alarms at ticks 1281 (54.29) and 1288 (54.99) occurred while CNC-05 was cutting job 15 (E6), i.e. brief cut-draw dips; once job 15 finished and CNC-05 went idle (E4), pressure recovered and stayed above the 55 bar setpoint — E7/E10 idle readings 1289-1302 range 55.96-58.25 bar with recovery from the 1297 low, no continued downward drift while idle. That idle recovery rules out H1 (seal leak predicts falling idle pressure toward/below 55). Smooth, mutually consistent trend across E5/E7/E10 rules out H3 (transducer fault). Persistent multi-bucket decline plus repeat sub-55 alarms rules out H4. Machine coverage is complete (E4/E2): only CNC-02 and CNC-05 have hydraulics; CNC-02 pressure is normal (screening [0.21, 0.2]), CNC-01/03/04/06 have no hydraulics. Inspections for CNC-05 jobs (batches 2, jobs 13-14) passed (E8), consistent with H2's 'some jobs still pass / failures grow with the leak.' No further check would change the diagnosis: more idle readings would just repeat E10, and waiting for CNC-05's next cut is uncertain and unnecessary since the sub-55-during-cut / recover-while-idle pattern is already observed.

[{"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a72.15", "text": "When to consult: A low hydraulic-pressure alarm; hydraulic pressure falling over many readings on one station; workpieces shifting or parts failing inspection on a station fitted with hydraulics. Possible causes: Leaking hydraulic seals, a weakening pump, a sticking relief valve, an instrument fault on the pressure transducer, or normal draw during a heavy cut. Recommended checks: Only some stations have hydraulics; the machine list shows which. The pump holds a steady pressure whenever the station is powered, running or idle, and cutting draws only a few bar from it, so a sound system reads nearly flat. When a station is down, its hydraulic unit and transducer are switched off and send no readings: missing samples then are not a pressure loss. A seal leak lowers the pressure slowly at first and then faster, and unlike wear on the spindle or the feed axis it keeps growing while the station sits idle, because the pump keeps running. The low-pressure alarm fires when a reading falls below its setpoint, which the alarm event states. Read the pressure trend over a long window that includes idle periods, and compare idle readings with idle readings: a fall that persists while the station is not cutting is a leak, not a heavy cut. A pressure loss does not change vibration, temperature, following error or job times, which separates it from a bearing (\u00a72.2), a drive (\u00a72.14) or a speed setting (\u00a72.7). Group inspection results by station and by batch as in \u00a72.14. An erratic reading with gaps and no matching quality change points at the transducer instead (\u00a72.11). How to interpret: Low clamping pressure lets the workpiece shift in the cut, so more jobs from that station fail inspection, and the share grows as the leak does; some of its jobs still pass (\u00a72.9). A falling pressure does not recover by itself, and readings that briefly return above the setpoint during idle or light work do not clear it: the leak keeps growing until the seals are replaced. The corrective action is an approved hydraulic repair, possible only on a station fitted with hydraulics, which takes it out of service for about 40 ticks to replace the seals; the maintenance record of the work states the condition of the seals removed. Afterwards the pressure should return to its steady level and that station's rejects should fall back; if they do not, look again.", "title": "Hydraulic Clamping: Pressure Loss, Seal Leaks and Repair"}, {"document": "SIM-CNC-001 rev 1.3", "section": "\u00a71.2", "text": "When to consult: A sensor exceeds an alarm value; averages disagree across windows; a trend looks erratic or has gaps. Possible causes: Operating changes, transient disturbances, instrument issues or developing equipment problems. Recommended checks: Compare vibration (mm/s), machine temperature (\u00b0F), motor load (%), and factory air temperature (\u00b0F) over the same relevant time window. Record ticks, sample counts, minimum and maximum, and a trend, not only the last reading. Separate running from idle periods. Link alarms to the underlying sensor readings and independent evidence. How to interpret: The default line vibration alarm is triggered by a reading above 4.5 mm/s. It is a monitoring setpoint, not a confirmed failure threshold. Missing samples are unknown, never zero. A sensor reading and a maintenance note are evidence; neither is a diagnosis. The evidence is sufficient to diagnose the anomaly. CNC-02's hydraulic pressure shows a clear, steady decline across all 30-tick blocks from 900 to 1049 (mean falling from 60.9 to 57.3 bar, minimum 54.46 bar at the alarm), while CNC-05 and CNC-07 remain flat near 68-69 bar over the same window. CNC-02's readings are steady with consistent sample counts (30 per block), not erratic with gaps. The other four machines have no hydraulics. This pattern matches the manual's description of a genuine leak or weakening pump (H1), refutes H2 (no recovery during idle/light blocks; pressure declines monotonically across cutting and waiting periods), and refutes H3 (readings are steady, not erratic/gappy). Inspection data (E8) is sparse—only two passed jobs, both before the major pressure drop—so it neither confirms nor refutes H1, but the pressure trend alone is decisive.
what could explain the evidence

Evidence settled: CNC-02 has a genuine, progressive hydraulic pressure loss (H1). CNC-02 block-mean hydraulic_pressure declines monotonically across the full window — 60.9 (900-929) → 59.9 → 59.1 → 58.6 → 57.3 bar (1020-1049), with block minimum 54.46 below the 55 bar alarm setpoint (E5, E9), while CNC-05 (~68-69) and CNC-07 (~68-69) stay flat over the same ticks (E6, E7). CNC-02 screening is far off baseline ([-13.21]) versus near-zero for CNC-05 ([0.02,-0.15]) and CNC-07 ([-0.37,-0.29]) (E2). CNC-02 readings are steady with complete samples and a consistent downward trend, not erratic/gappy (E5), refuting transducer fault H3; the multi-block monotonic decline refutes transient heavy-cut H2. Hydraulic-machine coverage is complete: CNC-01/03/04/06 have no hydraulics (E4), so no other machine can have a hydraulic fault. The only open question, Q4_updated/Q6 (CNC-02 vs CNC-05/CNC-07 inspection failure rate during the decline), cannot be answered from available data — only two inspections exist in 900-1050, both passed (E8), and their machines are unknown; the manual itself notes some jobs still pass under H1, so this does not change the diagnosis. No further call would alter the conclusion.
